site.landing.contact.bridge_text.text: Want to reach your device, and your friends, from outside your home network? Create an account on the <signup>account page</signup> or in your device's setup, and choose your address yourself. Need more than five addresses? Write to us with this form.

site.landing.contact.diy_text.text: Everything is documented in the <readme>README</readme> — architecture, config, and every install path.

site.landing.contact.lead.text: Send a message — whether it's a general question, help getting your device running, or more addresses for your bridge account.

site.landing.contact.message_placeholder.text: Tell us a bit about what you need

site.landing.contact.reason_addresses.text: More addresses for my bridge account

site.landing.contact.send_failed.text: Something went wrong sending your message.

site.landing.contact.sent.text: Thanks — we'll get back to you soon.

site.landing.contact.status_text.text: The device, the bridge and the web app work today, and so do the apps: iPhone and Android, the Mac app, and otc-sync for Windows and Linux.

site.landing.desktop.lead.text: Back up folders from your computer, or keep them the same on both sides. The apps sit in the menu bar or tray and update themselves: when a new version is out, one click installs it.

site.landing.desktop.linux_alt.text: ARM (e.g. a Raspberry Pi)? <linuxarm>Linux ARM64</linuxarm>. Then:

site.landing.desktop.linux_text.text: A tray app on a desktop, or a command line and a service on a server or a Pi.

site.landing.desktop.mac_button.text: Get it on the Mac App Store

site.landing.desktop.mac_text.text: A menu bar app with the same folders and sync rules, on the Mac App Store, which keeps it up to date for you.

site.landing.desktop.signed_note.text: Every update is signed. The apps only install a new version after checking its signature against the project's release key, the same key that signs the device updates. The source is on GitHub, and every file is listed on the desktop release.

site.landing.desktop.windows_alt.text: ARM PC? Windows on ARM. The app isn't code-signed yet, so Windows may warn you: choose More info → Run anyway.

site.landing.desktop.windows_text.text: Windows 10 or 11. Put the file somewhere permanent (not Downloads) and run it: it appears in the tray and starts at login.

site.landing.faq.ai.p1.text: On your device. The tagging model and the face models are downloaded once, when the software is installed, and run on the device's own processor; with several family accounts, the main one runs them for everyone. No photo is sent anywhere to be tagged or recognised, and place names come from a list of cities stored on the device, so your photos' locations aren't sent anywhere either.

site.landing.faq.ai.p2.text: Face recognition is off unless you turn it on, in the setup or in Settings, because faces are sensitive personal data. It looks at the photos added while it's on, and the face data it keeps is encrypted with your password like your files; the names you give people aren't. Tagging is on from the start and can be turned off in Settings.

site.landing.faq.ai.p3.text: Your photos leave the device only when you choose: when you post them for your friends, send a share link, or open them from your apps away from home, through the bridge.

site.landing.faq.ai.q.text: Where are photo tagging and face recognition done?

site.landing.faq.backup.p1.text: The two mirrored disks already keep two copies of everything, but both are in the same box: they protect you from one disk failing, not from theft, fire, both disks failing or a file deleted by mistake. For a copy you keep somewhere else, you can rotate one of the disks:

site.landing.faq.backup.p2.text: Until a copy has finished, your files are on one disk only, so never take out the other disk before then. While a disk is missing, the device takes any disk you plug in that is big enough as the replacement and erases it, so don't plug in other drives meanwhile.

site.landing.faq.backup.p3.text: The disk you keep is a full copy of the device as it was when you took it out: your files, its database, its settings and its address. A computer can't read it directly. To bring it back, set up a Raspberry Pi with the image, attach that disk and choose "Recover this device" in the setup: everything comes back as it was, and once you add a second disk the device fills it again. You need the device password as it was when the disk came out, because the files on it are encrypted with it. Use it only in place of the original device, never at the same time, since both would answer to the same address. The files on it are encrypted, but their names, tags and your posts aren't, so keep it as safe as you would the device itself.

site.landing.faq.backup.p4.text: Your phones and computers also keep their own copies: the apps copy your photos and folders to the device, they don't move them. To keep a copy of something on the device on a computer, select it in Files in the web app and choose Download ZIP, or add one of the device's folders to the Mac, Windows or Linux app. That is a sync, not a backup, so a file deleted on one side is deleted on the other.

site.landing.faq.backup.q.text: How do I back up my device?

site.landing.faq.backup.step1.text: While the device is running and nothing is uploading, take out one of the two disks. The device carries on with the other one, and you get an alert that a disk stopped working, which is expected here.

site.landing.faq.backup.step2.text: Put a spare disk in its place, at least as large as the one you took out. The device erases it and copies everything onto it by itself. When it's done you get another alert, "Both storage disks are working again"; that can take a few hours.

site.landing.faq.backup.step3.text: Keep the disk you took out somewhere safe, away from the device. To bring your copy up to date later, do the same again: the disk that comes out is your new copy, and the one going in is erased and refilled.

site.landing.faq.bridge.p1.text: Your device sits behind your home router, so the internet can't reach it on its own. The bridge is our relay at off-the.cloud: it gives your device an address like casa.off-the.cloud and passes connections from your apps and your friends' devices to it. You need it to reach your device away from home, for friends and posts, for share links that work from anywhere and for notifications on your phone. You don't need it at home: files, photo backup from your phones and computers, the gallery, tags and people all work over your own network.

site.landing.faq.bridge.p2.text: To use it, <signup>create an account</signup>; the device's setup asks for one, and you can also skip it and join later from Settings. Without the bridge, you can still reach your device from outside your home with Tailscale Funnel or a bridge of your own (see the next question).

site.landing.faq.bridge.q.text: What is "the Bridge", and do I need it?

site.landing.faq.family.p1.text: One device is enough. As its owner, you add an account for each person in Settings › Users (in the web app, the iPhone app or the Android app), and they choose their own password the first time they sign in. Each account has its own photo backup and library, and its photos and files are encrypted with that person's password, so you can't open them from your account. Everyone shares the same device and its two mirrored disks; the Users screen shows how much space each account takes, and you can pause an account, or remove it together with its files, at any time.

site.landing.faq.family.p2.text: There's no fixed limit on the number of accounts, but each one runs its own copy of the device's software and takes memory, so the more there are, the slower the device gets. We recommend no more than five on one device.

site.landing.faq.family.p3.text: To use their account away from home, a family member needs an off-the.cloud address of their own, just as a device does. You give them one when you add their account in the web app: in Settings › Users, leave Request bridge access ticked, and they get {address} (if that address is taken, choose another user name). Decide when you add the account, because there's no switch to give an existing account an address later. The iPhone and Android apps don't offer this yet: accounts added there work on your home network only.

site.landing.faq.family.p4.text: The device registers these addresses by itself, outside your bridge account, so they don't count toward its five addresses and don't appear on your account page. With one, a family member reaches their account from anywhere, and you can become friends in the private feed and share photos there.

site.landing.faq.family.q.text: Can my family and friends use the same device, or do I need more Raspberry Pis?

site.landing.faq.free.li1.text: Tailscale Funnel, built in (Settings › Tailscale Funnel), publishes your device at an address of your own on ts.net. You need a Tailscale account, Tailscale limits how much can pass through, and friends, posts and family accounts don't work there: it suits a device used as your own private storage.

site.landing.faq.free.li2.text: A bridge of your own: the bridge is open source too, so you can run it on your own server and domain. Friends then need to use the same bridge.

site.landing.faq.free.li3.text: Your own VPN into your home network: the apps then reach the device as if you were at home.

site.landing.faq.free.p1.text: Yes. All of Off The Cloud is free, open-source software under the GNU AGPL licence: the device, the apps and the bridge. Used at home it costs nothing beyond your hardware.

site.landing.faq.free.p2.text: The bridge is the only paid part, and it's optional. Your account is free for its first two years; after that it costs €9.99 + VAT a year with up to five off-the.cloud addresses included, and we email you before the free period ends. Each address beyond those five costs €2 a year: your account page registers up to five, so for more, write to us at <mail>info@off-the.cloud</mail> or with the <contact>form below</contact>. If you stop paying, your addresses are released and your device keeps working at home.

site.landing.faq.free.p3.text: To reach your device from outside your home without the bridge:

site.landing.faq.free.q.text: Can I use Off The Cloud for free?

site.landing.faq.friends_device.p1.text: Not necessarily. On your device you can add an account for each family member, or for a close friend, with their own photo backup, library and password. With an off-the.cloud address of its own, an account works from anywhere in the same apps and can be your friend in the feed. We recommend no more than five accounts on one device (see the question about family accounts below).

site.landing.faq.friends_device.p2.text: Friends who want their photos and files at home too set up a device of their own: the software is the same, and free. Everyone in the feed needs an off-the.cloud address, which comes with the bridge (see the question about the bridge below), unless you all use a bridge of your own. For people with no account at all, send a collection as a link: they open it in their browser, with no app.

site.landing.faq.friends_device.q.text: Do my friends and family need a device of their own?

site.landing.faq.from_google.p1.text: There's no Google Photos importer. Photos and videos still on your phone are backed up by the iPhone or Android app like any others, with their dates. For the rest, download your library with Google Takeout, unzip it on a computer and back up that folder with the <download>Mac, Windows or Linux app</download>: the photos and videos go to your device and appear in Images, tagged and searchable.

site.landing.faq.from_google.p2.text: Two things to know. Images puts each photo at its file's date, not the date it was taken, so photos from Takeout can end up in the wrong month; More info still shows the date stored in the photo, when it has one. And the .json files Takeout adds next to your photos, with each photo's date, description and place, aren't read: they're kept as ordinary files.

site.landing.faq.from_google.q.text: How do I move my photos from Google Photos?

site.landing.faq.from_icloud.p1.text: Use the iPhone app. When you sign in to your device, it asks which photos and videos to back up: choose "All photos and videos". Already signed in? Tap Sync All in Settings. "Sync from iCloud" is on from the start: when a photo's original is only in iCloud, as with "Optimise iPhone Storage", the iPhone downloads it first, then sends it to your device with its date.

site.landing.faq.from_icloud.p2.text: A whole library can take a long time and use a lot of data, so turn on "Wi-Fi only" if you'd rather not use mobile data. Backing up only copies your photos and leaves your iCloud library as it is: once your device has everything, what you keep in iCloud is up to you.

site.landing.faq.from_icloud.p3.text: The Mac app backs up folders, not the Photos library, so the iPhone, or an iPad on the same iCloud account, is the way to bring your library over.

site.landing.faq.from_icloud.q.text: How do I move my photos from iCloud?

site.landing.faq.hardware.a.text: A Raspberry Pi 5 (8GB) with a micro-SD card for the system and two USB drives for storage, mirrored so that each holds a full copy of your files: USB sticks, SSDs, hard disks or micro-SD cards in USB card readers all work. Plug them into the Pi's two blue USB ports (the fast ones; the device then tells you which one to replace if a drive ever fails). Add a power supply and an active cooler: all off-the-shelf. See the README for the exact recommended parts list. A Pi 5 with 4 GB can work too, with photo tagging and face recognition turned off.

site.landing.faq.hardware.q.text: Do I need to buy special hardware?

site.landing.faq.image.a.text: Yes — for a Raspberry Pi 5 with at least 8 GB of RAM (a 4 GB one works only with Image Tagging and Face Recognition turned off in Settings): see the <install>Raspberry Pi 5 image</install> tab at the top. Flash it, power the Pi on and set it up from your phone: tap "Set up a new device" in the iOS or Android app, which finds the Pi over Bluetooth and walks you through the rest. For any other Debian/Ubuntu machine, use the install script.

site.landing.faq.image.q.text: Is there a pre-built image I can just flash?

site.landing.faq.lights.caption.text: Pin 1 is the square one, at the end of the header farthest from the USB ports.

site.landing.faq.lights.p1.text: The lights are optional: one per storage disk, green when it's fine and red when it needs you. Each light is a red LED and a green LED side by side (or one two-colour LED with three legs), and each colour connects to one pin of the Raspberry Pi through a 330 Ω resistor. Wire them with the Pi switched off. The device lights them by itself; there's nothing to set up.

site.landing.faq.lights.p3.text: With a two-colour LED, the shared leg (usually the middle one) goes to GND; it must be the kind with a shared negative leg, called common cathode. What the lights say:

site.landing.faq.lights.p4.text: Each light follows one of the two disks of the mirror, not a USB port, so check the alert in the app to know which disk to pull.

site.landing.faq.lights.q.text: How do I wire the status lights?

site.landing.faq.lights.state1.text: Both green: both disks are working and hold the same files.

site.landing.faq.lights.state2.text: One red, one green: the disk on red has stopped working or was taken out. Your files are safe on the other one: replace the red one soon.

site.landing.faq.lights.state3.text: One flashing red, one green: a new disk is being filled with a copy of your files. Don't take out the green one until both are green again.

site.landing.faq.lights.state4.text: Both red: no mirror is running: the device was set up without two disks, or neither disk is working.

site.landing.faq.lights.state5.text: Both off: the device is off, or still starting.

site.landing.faq.lights.svg_desc.text: Pins 1 to 16 of the Raspberry Pi 5's 40-pin header, with pin 1 (3.3 volts, square) at the top and pins 17 to 40 continuing towards the USB ports. Light 1: pin 11 (GPIO17) through a 330 ohm resistor to the long leg of the red LED, and pin 13 (GPIO27) through a 330 ohm resistor to the long leg of the green LED; both short legs go to pin 9 (ground). Light 2: pin 15 (GPIO22) through a 330 ohm resistor to the red LED, and pin 16 (GPIO23) through a 330 ohm resistor to the green LED; both short legs go to pin 14 (ground). The same connections are listed below the drawing.

site.landing.faq.lights.svg_legs.text: + long leg of the LED · − short leg

site.landing.faq.lights.svg_more.text:
Pins 17–40 continue
towards the USB ports

site.landing.faq.lights.svg_resistor.text: Each small box is a 330 Ω resistor

site.landing.faq.lights.svg_title.text: Wiring the two status lights to the Raspberry Pi 5

site.landing.faq.lights.wire1.text: Light 1, red: pin 11 (GPIO17), through a 330 Ω resistor, to the long leg of the red LED.

site.landing.faq.lights.wire2.text: Light 1, green: pin 13 (GPIO27), through a 330 Ω resistor, to the long leg of the green LED.

site.landing.faq.lights.wire4.text: Light 2, red: pin 15 (GPIO22), through a 330 Ω resistor, to the long leg of the red LED.

site.landing.faq.lights.wire5.text: Light 2, green: pin 16 (GPIO23), through a 330 Ω resistor, to the long leg of the green LED.

site.landing.faq.open_source.a.text: Yes — the device, bridge, and every client are all open source on <github>GitHub</github>. You can audit it, self-host the bridge yourself, or build your own device image from source.

site.landing.faq.other_hw.li1.text: The ready-made image and setup from your phone over Bluetooth. Elsewhere you run one command in a terminal, and the first password typed into the device becomes its password, so open it and choose one straight away.

site.landing.faq.other_hw.li2.text: Knowing which disk to replace. On a Pi the alert names the USB port the failed disk is in; elsewhere it says "one of the two storage disks" and gives the disk's system name and serial number.

site.landing.faq.other_hw.li3.text: The status lights, which are wired to the Pi's own pins (see below).

site.landing.faq.other_hw.p1.text: Yes. The <install>install script</install> works on any 64-bit machine, Intel/AMD or ARM, running Ubuntu, Debian or another Debian-based Linux: an old PC or laptop, a mini PC, or a board such as an Orange Pi with a Debian or Ubuntu image. It builds the software on the machine itself, so you get the same app: photo backup, folder sync, photo tagging, face recognition, friends, sharing and updates from Settings. Give it 8 GB of memory, like the Raspberry Pi 5 it was designed for.

site.landing.faq.other_hw.p2.text: A few things only the Raspberry Pi 5 has:

site.landing.faq.other_hw.p3.text: The script can mirror two disks on other machines too, but only when you ask it to, because it erases both. If it finds no disks to mirror, it stops and tells you how to install on a single disk. To give the machine an off-the.cloud address, add the name on your <account>account page</account> first and copy the identity it shows into the machine before running the script.

site.landing.faq.other_hw.q.text: Can I use something other than a Raspberry Pi, like an Orange Pi or an old PC?

site.landing.faq.password.li1.text: Is one of your apps still signed in? Then it can still open everything, because it keeps the password. Don't sign out of it, and use it to copy what you need before going further.

site.landing.faq.password.li2.text: Look for your originals. The apps copy photos and folders to the device without removing them, so most of what's on it may still be on your phones and computers.

site.landing.faq.password.li3.text: Start again. Flash a new card and set the device up again, choosing "Start fresh instead" (this erases both disks), pick a new password and let your apps back everything up again.

site.landing.faq.password.li4.text: A family member forgot theirs? The owner can't reset it either. The only way is to remove their account, which deletes its files, and create it again.

site.landing.faq.password.p1.text: We're sorry: no. Your device password is the only thing that unlocks the key your files are encrypted with. The device doesn't keep it, neither do we, and there is no reset and no back door: without it, nobody can open the photos, videos and files stored under it, not you, not anyone else on the device and not us. That is what keeps them safe if the device is ever stolen.

site.landing.faq.password.p3.text: Your off-the.cloud account password is a different one: if you forget that, the account page emails you a link to reset it, and your device and files aren't affected. To avoid all this, keep your device password in a password manager or written down somewhere safe. You can change it in Settings at any time, as long as you know the current one, and your files stay as they are.

site.landing.faq.password.q.text: I forgot my password. Can I get my files back?

site.landing.faq.pi_dies.p1.text: Replace it with a new one and everything keeps working: your photos, files and settings are on the two USB drives, not on the Pi.

site.landing.faq.pi_dies.p2.text: Move the microSD card and the two drives to the new Pi and turn it on. If the card is lost too, flash a new one with the <install>Raspberry Pi 5 image</install>, attach the same drives and choose "Recover this device" in the setup: the device comes back as it was, with the same password. Don't choose "Start fresh instead", which erases both drives.

site.landing.faq.pi_dies.p3.text: If a drive dies instead, the device carries on with the other and tells you which one to replace.

site.landing.faq.pi_dies.q.text: What happens if the Raspberry Pi itself dies?

site.landing.faq.private.a.text: Your files are encrypted at rest with a key that only your password unlocks, and the password itself is never stored on the device. Photos and videos you post, and the posts your friends share with you, are the exception: they're kept unencrypted so your friends' devices can fetch them at any time. File names and tags are also kept readable so search works. Nothing is sold, used to train AI models, or shown to anyone you haven't chosen to share it with. The next two questions explain what the bridge and other services see, and where your photos are analysed.

site.landing.faq.protect.a.text: Yes: make it upload only, with the lock next to the folder in Files (in the web app, the iPhone app or the Android app). From then on nothing in that folder can be deleted, whether from a phone, a computer or the web, and when a file is uploaded again under the same name the device keeps the older version too, so an edit never overwrites your original. The Mac and Windows/Linux sync apps do this by themselves for a folder you choose to back up. You can clear it again from the same lock; the versions kept so far stay.

site.landing.faq.protect.q.text: Can I protect a folder from being deleted by mistake?

site.landing.faq.raw.p1.text: Yes. The device keeps every file exactly as it arrives: nothing is resized, converted or recompressed, so RAW files, HEIC photos and videos come back byte for byte.

site.landing.faq.raw.p2.text: The phone apps send each photo's and video's original file. On an iPhone, that means an edit made in Photos isn't backed up, only the original, and a Live Photo is backed up as its still photo.

site.landing.faq.raw.p3.text: For a camera's RAW files, back up the folder you copy them into with the <download>Mac, Windows or Linux app</download>: every file goes to the device as it is. The device makes a preview of some RAW files and tags those like any other photo; the others get no preview and don't show in Images, but they're kept all the same in Files.

site.landing.faq.raw.p4.text: What you post to your friends' feed can be a lighter copy: a large video is made smaller, and a HEIC photo goes as a JPEG. The original in your library stays as it was.

site.landing.faq.raw.q.text: Does it keep RAW files and videos in full quality?

site.landing.faq.social.a.text: It's entirely optional. Use OTC purely as a NAS for backup and file sync if that's all you want — the social feed only shows content from friends you've explicitly accepted.

site.landing.faq.social.q.text: What if I don't want the social network part?

site.landing.faq.social_how.p1.text: Everyone in it has an address of their own, like casa.off-the.cloud, and you add friends by their device's name. Once they accept, you see each other's posts in Social, in the phone apps and the web app: photos and videos with a caption, comments and likes, newest first, and a notification when someone likes or comments. Nothing is suggested or promoted, and there are no ads.

site.landing.faq.social_how.p2.text: Your posts are kept on your own device, and your friends' devices fetch them from it, so there's no central server holding everyone's posts. Devices reach each other through the bridge, which relays the connection without keeping anything that passes through. If you stop being friends, you can remove everything they shared from your device, and ask their device to delete what you shared there.

site.landing.faq.social_how.p3.text: There are no private messages or chats, on purpose: it leaves less room for bullying or for a stranger to approach a child. It's a feed for sharing photos and videos with the people you choose.

site.landing.faq.social_how.q.text: How does the private social network work?

site.landing.faq.speed.a.text: At home it's usually much faster. The iPhone, Android, Mac and Windows/Linux apps connect straight to your device over your own Wi-Fi or network, so backups, big uploads and videos move at local-network speed. A cloud service has to push every file through your home internet connection, whose upload speed is often a small fraction of your Wi-Fi's. Away from home, the apps go through the Bridge as usual. The home connection is encrypted and checked against your device's own key, so nothing is ever sent to a machine pretending to be yours.

site.landing.faq.speed.q.text: Is it as fast as a cloud service?

site.landing.faq.storage.a.text: Swap the two cards for bigger ones, one at a time, while the device keeps running. Take out one card and put in a bigger one, at least as large as the one you took out: the device copies everything onto it by itself (anything already on the new card is erased). You get an alert that a disk stopped working, which is expected here, and another, "Both storage disks are working again", when the copy is done; that can take a few hours for a large card. Only then do the same with the other card. Once both cards are bigger, the device grows its storage to the size of the smaller one by itself, within about ten minutes, without stopping. Your files stay available the whole time, but while a copy runs they are on one card only, so never take out the second card before the first copy has finished.

site.landing.faq.storage.q.text: How do I get more storage?

site.landing.faq.third_parties.bridge.text: The bridge (run by us, on OVH servers in France), if you use it: your account (email, name, surname and country), your devices' names (such as casa.off-the.cloud), when an app last reached each device, hourly traffic totals (never the content) and, for 90 days, the internet address of failed attempts to connect as your device. Connections to it are encrypted, and nothing that passes through is stored. A device without the bridge only contacts it during setup.

site.landing.faq.third_parties.github.text: GitHub serves the device's software and its updates; while installing or updating, the device also downloads building blocks from the Go language's mirror, run by Google, packages from its operating system's and Tailscale's repositories and, the first time, its AI models from Hugging Face and GitHub. Like any download, these see your home's internet address.

site.landing.faq.third_parties.maps.text: Maps: when you open a photo's details, its map comes from OpenStreetMap (web app and Android) or Apple Maps (iPhone), which see the place being shown.

site.landing.faq.third_parties.p1.text: Your photos, videos and files stay on your device. Nothing is sold, used for advertising or used to train AI, and none of the apps contain analytics, advertising or crash reporting. A few services are involved, and this is what each one gets:

site.landing.faq.third_parties.p2.text: There's no payment provider yet. The details are in our <privacy>privacy notice</privacy>.

site.landing.faq.third_parties.proton.text: Proton sends our emails (confirming your email, password resets, the warning before an unused account is removed) and delivers the device logs you choose to send us.

site.landing.faq.third_parties.push.text: Apple and Google deliver notifications to iPhones and Android phones. A notification only says who did what ("Anna liked your post") or that something happened to your device (a disk stopped working, it went offline), never what a post or comment says, and never a photo. The Android app uses Google's Firebase for this and nothing else. Notifications in a browser go through your browser maker's push service, encrypted.

site.landing.faq.third_parties.q.text: Is any of my information sent to third parties?

site.landing.faq.third_parties.signin.text: Apple or Google sign-in, if you use it, tells us your email and name.

site.landing.faq.third_parties.tailscale.text: Tailscale, only if you turn on Tailscale Funnel (its software is installed, but stays off until then).

site.landing.faq.vs_cloud.p1.text: Your photos live in your home instead of on a company's servers. You buy the hardware once instead of paying for a storage plan, and you have as much space as one of your two drives holds, since each keeps a full copy: when they fill up, you swap them for bigger ones.

site.landing.faq.vs_cloud.p2.text: Day to day it feels familiar. The phone apps back up your photos and videos in the background, in full resolution, and you can search them by what they show and, if you turn on face recognition, by who is in them. iPhones, Android phones and computers all work with it, with an account for each person in the family.

site.landing.faq.vs_cloud.p3.text: What changes is that you take ownership. Your photos are on two mirrored drives in your home, and a full backup is easy: take one drive out and put a new one in, and the device copies everything onto it; the drive you took out is your backup (see "How do I back up my device?"). Away from home, your apps reach it through the bridge (free for the first two years, then €9.99 + VAT a year), Tailscale Funnel or your own VPN. And there's no password reset: if you lose your device password, nobody can open your files, not even us.

site.landing.faq.vs_cloud.q.text: How is it different from Google Photos or iCloud?

site.landing.faq.vs_drive.p1.text: For your own files, yes. Files, in the web app and the phone apps, works like a drive: folders, uploads and downloads, moving and renaming, and share links that expire. The Mac, Windows and Linux apps keep chosen folders in two-way sync with the device or back them up, and a folder made upload-only can't have anything deleted from it and keeps the earlier version of a file uploaded again.

site.landing.faq.vs_drive.p2.text: You get as much space as one of your two drives holds, with no plan to upgrade: when they fill up, you swap them for bigger ones.

site.landing.faq.vs_drive.q.text: Can it replace Google Drive, Dropbox or Proton Drive?

site.landing.faq.vs_instagram.p1.text: Instagram and Facebook are free because advertising pays for them: your posts are kept on Meta's servers, an algorithm ranks what you see, and Meta uses public posts and comments to train its AI unless you object. On Off The Cloud your posts are on your own device, only the friends you accept see them, the feed is simply newest first, and nothing is used for ads or to train AI.

site.landing.faq.vs_instagram.p2.text: It's also made for a smaller circle: not for building an audience or following strangers, but for the family and friends you'd show your photos to at home.

site.landing.faq.vs_instagram.q.text: How is it different from Instagram or Facebook?

site.landing.faq.vs_selfhosted.li1.text: It installs from an app: the computer app prepares the Raspberry Pi's card, and the setup finishes over Bluetooth from your phone or Mac, with no terminal.

site.landing.faq.vs_selfhosted.li2.text: It runs on inexpensive hardware: a Raspberry Pi 5 and two USB pen drives, mirrored, with alerts that say which one to replace.

site.landing.faq.vs_selfhosted.li3.text: Files encrypted at rest, with a key only your password unlocks.

site.landing.faq.vs_selfhosted.li4.text: It's a NAS for your files too, kept in two-way sync with your computers, not only a photo library.

site.landing.faq.vs_selfhosted.li5.text: A private social network between friends' devices, with no ads and no algorithm, which Immich and PhotoPrism don't have.

site.landing.faq.vs_selfhosted.li6.text: Apps for phones and computers, an account for each person in the family, and an optional bridge to reach it from anywhere without opening ports on your router.

site.landing.faq.vs_selfhosted.p1.text: Immich and PhotoPrism are photo libraries and Nextcloud is a file and collaboration suite. They're free and open source, but they're made for people who run their own server: you install them yourself, usually with Docker on a Linux machine, and work out storage, backups and remote access on your own.

site.landing.faq.vs_selfhosted.p2.text: Off The Cloud is easier to install and needs almost no technical knowledge, and it does more than photos:

site.landing.hero.demo_note.text: Look around a real device with a made-up family's photos and files. No sign-up.

site.landing.hero.lead.text: Off The Cloud is a private social network for your family and friends, and a home for your photos and files, on a small device you own. Post photos and videos, comment and like, with no ads, no algorithm and no strangers: your posts stay on your device and go only to the devices of friends you accept, never stored on a company's servers. The same device backs up everyone's phones in full resolution and keeps your computers' folders in sync, so it takes the place of Instagram, Google Photos, iCloud, Google Drive and Dropbox at once. It's free, open-source software for a Raspberry Pi 5, set up from your phone.

site.landing.hero.pill.text: 100% open source · social network, photos and files on your own device

site.landing.install.app_intro.text: The easiest way: the app downloads the image and checks its signature, writes the card itself on Windows and Linux, and guides you through each step.

site.landing.install.app_more.text: ARM versions, and first-run tips for Windows and Linux, are in the <download>download section</download>.

site.landing.install.app_step_card.text: Make the card. The app downloads the image and checks it against the project's signature. On Windows and Linux it then writes it to a MicroSD card of 8 GB or more, after asking for administrator permission; on a Mac it opens Raspberry Pi Imager to write the card and tells you what to choose there.

site.landing.install.app_step_open.text: Install the app and choose Set Up a New Device…: in the Mac app's Settings, or in the tray menu on Windows and Linux.

site.landing.install.app_step_setup.text: Finish the setup over Bluetooth. On a Mac, right in the app: On this Mac (or use your phone). On Windows and Linux, in the phone app (iOS or Android): tap Set up a new device. Either way it asks for your WiFi, a name and password for the device and how to use the disks, then installs the software - about 20 minutes.

site.landing.install.bridge_link.text: Want to reach it from outside your home network? Create an account for the bridge →

site.landing.install.image_note.text: The image only carries the setup wizard: it installs the current release, so it never goes out of date. Checksum: <sha>.sha256</sha>.

site.landing.install.requirements.text: For a Raspberry Pi 5 with at least 8 GB of RAM, a MicroSD card for the system and, optionally, two USB disks for RAID-1, plugged into the Pi's two blue USB ports. Use the official Raspberry Pi 27 W USB-C power supply (or a better one): with a weaker one the Pi can restart from low voltage while it processes your photos. No keyboard, monitor or Linux knowledge needed. Only have a 4 GB Pi? It can run, but only with Image Tagging and Face Recognition turned off in Settings, before you back up your photos: those models need more memory than 4 GB leaves.

site.landing.install.script_intro.text: One command on any machine you can already log into: Ubuntu, Debian, Raspberry Pi OS and other Debian-based distros (64-bit).

site.landing.install.script_note.text: It installs everything and builds the software from source, then starts the service at {address}. Safe to re-run to update. Your files go on two disks mirrored as RAID-1: it reuses a mirror it finds and only erases two new disks to build one when you confirm it, and it installs the status lights too. A single disk works as well (see the README). The WiFi setup isn't part of this path — see the image for a from-scratch Raspberry Pi.

site.landing.install.step_flash.text: Flash it to the MicroSD card with Raspberry Pi Imager: "Use custom", pick the file, write. Skip Imager's own customisation step.

site.landing.install.step_plug.text: Plug in the disks (into the two blue USB ports), insert the card and power the Pi on. After a minute it announces itself over Bluetooth.

site.landing.install.step_setup.text: Set it up from your phone with the app (iOS or Android): on the welcome screen tap Set up a new device. It finds the Pi over Bluetooth and runs the setup right there - your phone stays on its own WiFi. It asks for your WiFi, a name and password for the device and how to use the disks, then installs the software - about 20 minutes.

site.landing.install.step_signin.text: Sign in when it's done: the app connects to the new device by itself with the password you chose, or open {address} in a browser.

site.landing.started.lead.text: Both paths end in the same place: the image just runs the install script for you, after asking for your WiFi, a name and your disks from a phone.

site.landing.started.note.text: Starting from scratch on a Raspberry Pi 5? Use the Raspberry Pi 5 image: it wipes and mirrors two USB disks during setup, and if a Pi ever dies you flash a new card, attach the same disks and the wizard offers to recover everything. The status LEDs and every configuration option are in the README.

site.landing.started.step1_text.text: It installs MariaDB, Go, ONNX Runtime and the tagging model, then builds and starts the otc service, reachable straight away at {address} on your local network — safe to re-run any time to pick up updates.

site.landing.started.step2_text.text: This names the device, e.g. pit for pit.off-the.cloud — the address your apps and friends use to reach it from outside your home network, instead of the local :8080 address. Register the name on your account page first, so it belongs to your bridge account (the image's setup does this for you).

site.landing.started.step3_text.text: Open the web, iOS, Android, macOS, Windows or Linux client, point it at your subdomain, and start backing up.

site.landing.what.decentral_text.text: Every family's posts live on its own device, and friends' devices fetch them from each other. There's no central server holding everyone's photos, so there's nothing to sell, mine or leak in one place.

site.landing.what.desktop_text.text: macOS, Windows and Linux apps that keep chosen folders on your computer in two-way sync with the device, automatically.

site.landing.what.device_text.text: A Raspberry Pi 5 with a microSD card for the system and two USB drives mirrored in RAID-1, storing your originals exactly as they arrive, never resized or recompressed — encrypted at rest, with a key that only your password unlocks.

site.landing.what.family_text.text: Give everyone at home their own account on the same device — their own photo backup, library and password, each encrypted with its own key. You manage the accounts, but you can't open the photos and files in them.

site.landing.what.fast_text.text: At home the apps talk straight to the device over your own network, so a whole holiday's photos back up at Wi-Fi speed instead of crawling over the internet.

site.landing.what.feed_text.text: Post photos and videos for your family and friends, with captions, comments, likes and notifications. Only the friends you've accepted see them, newest first: no ads, no influencers and no algorithm deciding what you see.

site.landing.what.files_text.text: Keep folders from every computer in two-way sync or backed up, open and share them from your phone, and lock a folder so nothing in it can be deleted and earlier versions are kept.

site.landing.what.lead.text: One small device in your home keeps your family's posts, photos and files. Apps on every platform keep it in sync and let you browse, search and share it.

site.landing.what.mobile_text.text: iOS and Android apps for your social feed, notifications and photo backup: they back up your camera roll in the background, in full resolution.

site.landing.what.photos_text.text: The phone apps back up every photo and video in the background, as the original, so your library is complete and in full quality, with no storage plan to outgrow.

site.landing.what.search_text.text: Every photo is auto-tagged locally on the device, so you can search "beach" or "dog" instantly — nothing is sent to a third party to do it.

site.landing.what.share_text.text: Send a collection of photos to anyone as a link that expires. They open it in their browser, with no account or app, and can download the originals.

site.landing.what.title.text: A social network, a photo library and a NAS, in one device

site.landing.what.web_text.text: Everything above, from any browser — sign in with just your password, no app install required.
